material.text: human-hindsight: Mine coding-agent history (Claude Code, Codex, Kiro, OpenCode) into a oneshot prompt library and CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md preferences. The prompt you'd write if you knew then what you know now.

# Human Hindsight > **The prompt you'd write if you knew then what you know now.** [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/human-hindsight?color=cb3837&logo=npm)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/human-hindsight) [![CI](https://github.com/adityaarunsinghal/human-hindsight/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/adityaarunsinghal/human-hindsight/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![node](https://img.shields.io/node/v/human-hindsight?logo=node.js&color=339933)](https://nodejs.org) [![license](https://img.shields.io/github/license/adityaarunsinghal/human-hindsight?color=blue)](LICENSE) [![local-first](https://img.shields.io/badge/data-local--only-brightgreen)](#privacy--trust)

```bash npx human-hindsight@latest ``` Human Hindsight mines your coding-agent session history (Claude Code, Codex, Kiro, OpenCode) into two things you can use tomorrow morning: 1. **A oneshot prompt library.** For each real task you've done, the realistic ideal *first* prompt: everything you knew and wanted at t=0 but didn't say, written in your own voice. 2. **A distilled preference set.** The things you keep re-telling your agent ("diagnose before acting", "pin the versions", "be terse"), surfaced as a paste-ready `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` block so every future session starts aligned. Previously published as **cc-hindsight**. The `cc-hindsight` npm package is now a deprecated compatibility command that forwards to the matching Human Hindsight release. Existing libraries, edits, ratings, and checkpoints remain usable. ### Upgrading from cc-hindsight ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest gui # Or install the new command globally: npm install -g human-hindsight ``` No data move or re-distillation is required. Data-directory precedence is: `--home` → `HUMAN_HINDSIGHT_HOME` → legacy `CC_HINDSIGHT_HOME` → an existing `~/.human-hindsight` → an existing `~/.cc-hindsight` → `~/.human-hindsight` for a fresh installation. If both directories exist, the new one wins; use `--home` to choose explicitly. Directories are never merged automatically. In 1.8.2, existing preferences remain visible as **candidates**. Open the Preferences tab, check the evidence and scope, then **Accept**, **Edit**, or **Dismiss** each candidate. **Accepted instructions** builds a block from accepted global rules, with an optional project selection. Task-only choices stay out of standing instruction files. Reviews are saved in your library and survive browser restarts. Re-running `distill` refreshes results whose source content, prompt version, runner/model selection, or grouping mode changed. Older checkpoints are refreshed once because they have no input fingerprints. Hand-edited prompts are preserved; `--force` explicitly allows replacing them. Updating the old npm package installs the small compatibility wrapper, so `npx cc-hindsight@latest gui` also works. Both global commands can coexist: the main package owns `human-hindsight`, and the wrapper owns `cc-hindsight`. The GitHub repository was renamed in place; old repository links redirect. ### Retrying unfinished distillation Choose the mode that matches the work you want to do: | Command | Work selected | Existing grouping and successful prompts | |---|---|---| | `distill` | Normal refresh using current inputs and settings | May refresh affected results and grouping | | `distill --retry-failed` | Recorded failed or interrupted operations, and recorded blockers that are now resolved | Preserved | | `distill --recover-tasks=slug-a,slug-b` | Explicitly named saved tasks from an older run without failure history | Preserved; authoring only | Preview strict retry before spending: ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest distill --retry-failed --dry-run npx human-hindsight@latest distill --retry-failed # Narrow the retry to recorded authoring failures: npx human-hindsight@latest distill --retry-failed --retry-stage=author ``` `--retry-stage` accepts `all` (the default), `digest`, `cluster`, or `author`. A recovered digest does not trigger clustering or authoring. A recovered cluster result is saved for adoption by a later normal `distill`; retry never replaces the saved task grouping. Successful operations and work never attempted are excluded, even when you override the model or input budget. Older runs have no recorded failure history. Select their saved task slugs explicitly instead of inferring failures from missing files: ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest distill \ --recover-tasks=slug-a,slug-b --runner=claude \ --input-budget=600000 --dry-run ``` Use real slugs from your saved grouping, then repeat without `--dry-run` to reach consent. Existing successful or manually edited prompts are protected. Both recovery modes show selected work, local repairs, exclusions, and blockers. Strict retry requires unchanged recorded inputs and compatible operation records; legacy recovery requires the saved task and its source evidence. A changed or missing input can require a normal refresh. Neither mode combines with `--fresh`, `--force`, or explicit grouping, project, source, or substance filters. The default input budget remains **400,000 content characters**; `600000` is an explicit override, not a guarantee that a provider accepts the request. Digest and author calls default to **900 seconds**. Clustering and preference consolidation add five seconds per input item to that base. An explicit `--timeout=N` uses exactly N seconds. Strict retry inherits recorded attempt settings unless explicitly overridden; a previously default timeout follows the current default. Review the effective settings in the preview. ## The t=0 problem You get better results the more context you front-load into your first prompt, yet we underspecify at t=0 and spend the session steering: correcting course, restating preferences, answering questions the agent shouldn't have had to ask. And the cost repeats every session. Your working preferences are stable facts about how you like to work, yet you re-derive and re-type them project after project instead of stating them once, upfront, where every future session reads them from the first message. All the evidence of what you *should* have said is already on disk. Claude Code saves session JSONL under `~/.claude/projects/`; Codex keeps rollouts under `~/.codex/sessions/` and `~/.codex/archived_sessions/`; kiro-cli keeps its own store under `~/.kiro/sessions` (both the flat `cli/.jsonl` layout and the newer per-session `/sess_/messages.jsonl` layout). OpenCode keeps its SQLite history under `~/.local/share/opencode/`. Plenty of tools read that data for dashboards and transcripts. **Nobody closes the loop from history back to better prompting.** **Before** (what you actually typed at t=0): > help me script blocking a device on my home router **After** (what human-hindsight distilled from how that session actually went): > I want to automate my home router, starting with blocking a device. Get API > access working first, and store any credentials securely instead of asking me > to paste them in the clear. Anything that changes the network should be safe > by default: show me what it'll do and let me confirm before it runs. Then > prove it end-to-end on a real device. Research how others have done this > first, and keep the setup written down so I can reproduce it. The second prompt was knowable at t=0. You just hadn't written it yet. ## Quickstart Start the guided terminal workflow: ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest ``` After scanning, the CLI suggests **export** and asks whether to run it. Type `y` to continue. Export offers **distill**, and a successful distillation offers the browser library. Your library directory, source, project filter, runner, and model stay selected through the handoffs. Distillation still shows its model-call plan and asks for spending consent. Follow-up offers default to No and appear only in an interactive terminal. Use `--no-follow-up` for one command at a time; pipes, dry runs, and scripted `--yes` invocations never start these follow-up commands automatically. You can also start directly with distillation: ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest distill # offers to export first, then digest → cluster → # author (asks before any runner call), then shows # offers the finished library in your browser ``` Prefer to drive each stage yourself? The pipeline is just three verbs: ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest # 1. scan: inventory your projects (read-only) npx human-hindsight@latest export # 2. export: human-only markdown per session npx human-hindsight@latest distill # 3. distill: digest → cluster → author (asks first) ``` Then browse and curate the results: ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest list # your library (✎ edited / ▲▼ rating badges) npx human-hindsight@latest gui # browse, search, and copy in your browser npx human-hindsight@latest show # read a oneshot npx human-hindsight@latest copy # → clipboard, paste into a fresh session npx human-hindsight@latest edit # open in $EDITOR; your edits are protected npx human-hindsight@latest rate up # record a verdict (up|down) npx human-hindsight@latest prune # remove orphaned entries (asks first) npx human-hindsight@latest preferences # accepted global rules → CLAUDE.md npx human-hindsight@latest preferences --project my-app # include this project's accepted rules npx human-hindsight@latest status # pipeline funnel + orphan/skip flags npx human-hindsight@latest retention # optional: preview longer local retention ``` Requires Node 22.13+ on Node 22, or Node 23.4+ on newer releases, on macOS or Linux (Windows is untested and currently unsupported). `scan` and `export` are fully deterministic: no LLM, no network. `distill` uses your installed `claude`, `codex`, `kiro-cli`, or `opencode`, with a consent prompt (or your explicit `--yes`). ### A small local library viewer ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest gui # start locally and open your browser npx human-hindsight@latest gui --no-open # print the address without opening it npx human-hindsight@latest gui --port 3210 # choose a port (default: any available port) npx human-hindsight@latest gui --home /path/to/library-home ``` Switch between **Prompts** and **Preferences** to search, filter by domain, sort, and copy items with one click. Preferences are deduplicated across tasks and can be sorted by frequency, recency, or text. Search also matches their evidence and source prompt titles. One expandable domain tree lets you browse from broad categories down to five levels. Select a parent to include its descendants, or expand its arrow to choose a child. Prompt details show shared ancestry once; open **+N** to see the full grouped hierarchy. Domain labels from the same evidence are deduplicated regardless of casing. Existing flat labels are grouped locally without changing the library or making a model call; newly distilled sessions use hierarchical domain paths. **Preview** renders Markdown headings, lists, tables, links, blockquotes, task lists, and code blocks. **Markdown** shows the original source. Copy always uses that original Markdown, including when the preview is selected. Each prompt links to its preference candidates. Newly distilled candidates show exact human quotations, message references, and global/project/task scope; older observations are labeled for review. Open the collapsed **Source evidence** section to see quotations. Use the check, pencil, and dismiss icons to review a candidate; each control has an accessible label and hover description. Candidates can come from failed or unfinished sessions too. You can bookmark either view and use your browser's Back and Forward buttons. **All** shows observations; **Accepted** provides the reviewed instruction block for `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`. Changed source evidence returns a candidate to review. The terminal `preferences` command also exports accepted rules by default. Use `--include-unreviewed` explicitly to inspect draft observations in scripts. This flag does not accept them or change their review status. A compact tip card sits in the header and flips through quick suggestions. Open it to read the explanation, copy a `npx human-hindsight@latest` command, or pause or hide tips. The lightbulb restores hidden tips. Rotation pauses while you interact, and reduced-motion settings disable the flip animation. Hidden tips stay hidden when you reload the same local address. Export and distill show an open-source/privacy reminder near the start. Interactive terminals get a colorful elapsed-time progress indicator during scanning, export, and model work; redirected output stays free of animation. Consolidation is optional: `npx human-hindsight@latest preferences --consolidate` uses your accepted rules in a call through your own coding harness and its configured provider, with consent and the subscription/credit cost explained first. Successful results are saved, with their Markdown and input metadata, in `/library/preferences.consolidated.json`. Reload the browser and select **Saved** to open the consolidation. Every output rule links to its input preferences. Coverage, scope, explicit conditions, and direct contradictions are checked; invalid output gets one semantic correction attempt. Failed, empty, incomplete, or declined results leave the last saved result intact. Saved results are flagged when the selected inputs or their review status change. Legacy saved results remain readable and need regeneration before copying as reviewed instructions. The viewer uses a minimal black-and-white palette and system monospace fonts. Light and dark appearance follow your system setting. Rows emphasize titles; session counts remain visible, and the information icon reveals dates, confidence, local edits, and ratings. Reload the browser after changing files and press `/` to focus search. The GUI uses Node's built-in HTTP server and bundled HTML/CSS/JavaScript: no frontend framework, database, font download, or external assets. Markdown parsing and sanitization ship inside the bundle. Raw HTML stays inert and remote images are represented by their alt text, without fetching them. It listens only on `127.0.0.1` and stops with Ctrl+C. Browsing stays read-only. The single write action saves an explicit preference review to `library/preferences.review.json`; it requires the current browser session's token, matching origin, and a current candidate revision. The GUI never invokes an agent, edits source history, or writes an instruction file for you. ### Multiple backends (Claude Code + Codex + Kiro + OpenCode) Every command takes `--source claude|codex|kiro|opencode|auto` (default `auto`: read whichever stores exist). Select the source after the subcommand. Directory flags work before or after it: | Source | Directory flag | Environment variable | Default | |---|---|---|---| | Claude Code | `--claude-dir` | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` | `~/.claude` | | Codex | `--codex-dir` | `CODEX_HOME` | `~/.codex` | | kiro-cli | `--kiro-dir` | `KIRO_CONFIG_DIR` | `~/.kiro` | | OpenCode | `--opencode-dir` | `HUMAN_HINDSIGHT_OPENCODE_DIR`, then `XDG_DATA_HOME` | `~/.local/share/opencode` | For OpenCode, `--opencode-db` selects a database explicitly; relative names resolve under the data directory. It overrides `HUMAN_HINDSIGHT_OPENCODE_DB` and OpenCode's `OPENCODE_DB`, with `opencode.db` as the default. An in-memory database has no persisted history to read. Configuration is separate: `OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` or the XDG config directory, normally `~/.config/opencode`. Human Hindsight's directory/database flags select source history; the OpenCode runner uses the CLI's normal data location and authentication. Multiple stores merge into one library; the manifest tags each session's `origin` and the export summary breaks the count down. Codex discovery includes active and archived rollouts from the CLI, IDE extension, and app, grouped by their working directory. Mirrored user/assistant events are paired, injected context and subagent sessions are excluded, and human decisions and images survive extraction. The kiro backend reads both on-disk store layouts (the flat v2 store and the newer v3 per-session store), preferring the v3 copy when a session was migrated into both. `distill --runner claude|codex|kiro|opencode|auto` chooses which CLI does the distilling, independently of `--source`. `auto` prefers the CLI matching an explicit source, then falls back in the order Claude → Codex → Kiro → OpenCode. Models are passed through with `--model`; without it, the chosen CLI uses its configured default. ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest export --source codex npx human-hindsight@latest distill --source codex --runner codex npx human-hindsight@latest distill --source claude --runner codex npx human-hindsight@latest preferences --target codex # AGENTS.md; alias of --target agents npx human-hindsight@latest export --source opencode npx human-hindsight@latest distill --source opencode --runner opencode npx human-hindsight@latest distill --source claude --runner opencode --model provider/model npx human-hindsight@latest preferences --target opencode # AGENTS.md ``` `preferences --target claude|codex|kiro|opencode|agents` emits a `CLAUDE.md` block, an `AGENTS.md` section, or a block for `~/.kiro/steering/`. An explicit Codex source defaults to `AGENTS.md`. The Codex runner uses `codex exec` with a JSON schema, a read-only sandbox, and ephemeral sessions; generated distill sessions do not become new source history. Claude supports current `structured_output` results as well as legacy `result` objects/strings and verbose event arrays. The Claude runner requires current isolation controls, including `--safe-mode`. It runs from a private directory, disables tools, hooks, skills, and ambient MCP configuration, supplies a dedicated system instruction, and disables session persistence. Unsupported CLIs fail before any model call with an upgrade hint or the option to choose another runner. Updating Human Hindsight does not update Claude Code. Organization-managed policy remains authoritative; these controls do not override administrator policy or constitute an operating-system sandbox. ### OpenCode 1 and 2 OpenCode support covers both current release families: `opencode-ai` 1.19 (verified with 1.19.4) and `@opencode/cli` 2.1 (verified with 2.1.3). Both install an `opencode` command. Source discovery does not need the CLI. The reader handles OpenCode 1's session/message/part SQLite tables, OpenCode 2's ordered message records, and recognized older `storage/session`, `storage/message`, and `storage/part` JSON directories. It includes archived sessions, preserves question answers and attachment markers, and excludes generated subagent and distillation sessions. Completed compaction resets short-reply context; explicit execution failures are included in the outcome evidence. Read-only SQLite connections include committed WAL data. Human Hindsight never migrates the source database. An unreadable, busy, unsupported, or incompletely migrated OpenCode database stops export before replacing the manifest or pruning existing exports. If migrated copies coexist, matching human turns are deduplicated; divergent older copies keep distinct export names. Reverted tails are excluded. Only committed conversation messages are read, not pending inbox items. The OpenCode runner uses JSON events, validates the final answer, and permits one corrective retry. It copies provider/model settings from JSON or JSONC into an owner-only temporary configuration, while OpenCode continues to handle credentials. Project instructions, external agent plugins, and MCP configuration are not copied. A dedicated agent denies tools; OpenCode 2 uses an owned private server. Providers that require external agent plugins may need a built-in or compatible provider configuration for this runner. Generated sessions are marked and excluded from future exports. After the run, cleanup deletes only captured IDs whose title and working directory prove they belong to that run. Interrupted runs or cleanup failures can leave marked sessions behind. User settings and unrelated sessions are preserved. OpenCode preferences can go into the project's `AGENTS.md`, or the global `AGENTS.md` under your OpenCode config directory. ### Optional: keep more local history ```bash npx human-hindsight@latest retention # read-only preview npx human-hindsight@latest retention --apply # preview, then confirm npx human-hindsight@latest retention --apply --yes # explicit opt-in for scripting npx human-hindsight@latest retention --source codex --apply ``` The default reviews existing tool directories. An explicit `--source` can create that tool's settings file. `--yes` alone never applies changes, and `--dry-run` always keeps the command read-only. - **Claude Code:** raises `cleanupPeriodDays` to 365,000 days (about 1,000 years), preserving an already longer value. Claude requires a positive whole number; `0` is invalid. If desktop cleanup is capped, sets `desktopSessionCleanupPeriodDays` to `0`, its supported no-age-limit value. An absent desktop setting already has no age limit. - **Codex:** sets `[history] persistence = "save-all"` and removes `history.max_bytes`, leaving prompt history uncapped. This controls `history.jsonl`; full session rollouts are stored separately. Avoid `--ephemeral` for your own sessions you want to retain. - **kiro-cli:** explains automatic persistence and `/chat save ` for additional copies. Its public settings reference does not document a retention-limit switch, so no configuration key is invented. - **OpenCode:** reports the local data/config locations and archival guidance. No supported full-session age/size retention setting is documented. OpenCode 2 keeps earlier messages after compaction and ignores the older `compaction.prune` setting. Temporary overflow tool-output files have separate cleanup (seven days in 2.1); output-size limits do not change that lifetime. This integration is advisory and leaves compaction settings untouched. For an extra copy, use `opencode session export ` on OpenCode 2 or `opencode export ` on OpenCode 1. Applying creates owner-only backups next to existing configuration files, then replaces each file atomically. Other settings are preserved; common Codex TOML layouts retain comments, while unusual layouts may be reformatted after a preview notice. Malformed configurations are left untouched. Longer retention keeps prompt contents on disk longer and can use more space. Restart running tools after applying settings. Project settings, profiles, managed policy, and startup flags can override user defaults; this command does not change those controls, remote retention, or telemetry. It cannot recover already deleted history. Setting references: [Claude retention](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#cleanupperioddays), [Codex configuration](https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-reference), and [Kiro conversation persistence](https://kiro.dev/docs/cli/chat/). OpenCode references, pinned to the supported v2 release: [compaction](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.1.3/services/www/src/docs/content/compaction.mdx), [migration](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.1.3/services/www/src/docs/content/migrate-v1.mdx), and [session commands](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/v2.1.3/services/www/src/docs/content/cli/commands.mdx). ## Privacy & trust For a tool that reads your entire conversation history, auditability is the product: - **Local-only.** Everything is read from your disk and written to your disk (`~/.human-hindsight`). No hosted service, accounts, or telemetry. The only network traffic is through your chosen agent CLI during consented distillation or preference consolidation. - **One self-contained npm package.** JavaScript libraries are bundled into the CLI; the published package has no npm dependencies or installation scripts. SQLite comes from Node. Starting the app does not install compilers, platform bindings, or build tools. The development dependency tree is pinned in the repository's `package-lock.json`, which is not published. Bundled libraries include citty, Zod, Clack, smol-toml, jsonc-parser, Marked, and DOMPurify; their license texts ship in `dist/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`. - **Consent-gated LLM use.** `distill` states its estimated invocation count and waits for `[y/N]` before anything runs on your subscription/credits. `--dry-run` shows the full plan for free. If you decline, it exits without invoking anything (exit code 2). - **Plain statement:** exports contain your raw prompts, including anything sensitive you ever pasted into a session (keys, internal names, that one angry message). They live in your home directory with your permissions, and nothing ships them anywhere. A `--redact` option is on the roadmap. ## How it works ```mermaid flowchart TD A["~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl"] -->|"scan (read-only)"| B["inventory"] X["~/.codex/{sessions,archived_sessions}/**/rollout-*.jsonl"] --> B K["~/.kiro/sessions/"] --> B O["~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db"] --> B A -->|"export (deterministic)"| C["exports/*.md + manifest.json"] X --> C K --> C O --> C A -->|"anaphora + outcome evidence"| D["anaphora.json + outcomes.json"] X --> D K --> D O --> D C --> E D --> E subgraph distill ["distill: opt-in, consent-gated, resumable"] E["digest: 1 runner call / session"] --> F["cluster: 1 call"] F --> G["author: 1 call / task"] end G --> H["library/<slug>/ oneshot + provenance"] H --> I["list / show / copy / status"] H --> J["preferences → CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / Kiro steering"] ``` The extraction layer is a fidelity contract: eleven audited rules decide what counts as human input (attachments typed while the agent was busy, recovered slash commands, `[decision]` lines from option picks, `[image pasted]` markers), with a regression fixture per rule. Fork/resume duplicates are deduped globally. Short replies like "yes" and "option 2" get their antecedent attached so the author stage knows what you approved. Sessions carry an outcome classification, so a task where nothing ever succeeded gets skipped instead of becoming a confident prompt that reproduces a failure path. Authored oneshots pass a **"knowable at t=0" test**: they front-load intent, constraints, preferences, and quality bars, while leaving out facts you only discovered mid-session (paths, root causes, error messages). And they respect an **effort budget**, staying around the length a motivated human would actually type rather than ballooning into a 700-word spec. Distillation records operation progress and saves validated results before publishing outputs. Strict retry can recover saved results locally and retry recorded failures without rerunning successes. A provider response lost before it is saved may still need another call. Normal `distill` refreshes changed work, `--fresh` resets deliberately, and `status` flags library entries orphaned by re-clustering. ## How it compares | Tool | Reads `~/.claude` | Output | Direction | |---|---|---|---| | ccusage | ✓ | usage/cost tables | backward (metrics) | | sniffly | ✓ | analytics dashboard | backward (behavior) | | claude-code-transcripts | ✓ | shareable HTML transcripts | backward (record) | | cctrace / exporters | ✓ | markdown/XML exports | backward (archive) | | **human-hindsight** | ✓ | **oneshot prompt library + CLAUDE.md preferences** | **forward (better next session)** | Closest kin is Simon Willison's `claude-code-transcripts`: same local-first values, same belief that transcripts are undervalued artifacts. The difference is the direction of gaze: it renders your sessions (backward, for others); human-hindsight distills them (forward, for you). ## FAQ **Does my data leave my machine?** The deterministic commands (`scan`, `export`, and `retention`) never touch the network. `distill` and `preferences --consolidate` send content through your chosen local agent CLI to its configured provider, using its authentication. **What does distill cost?** Whatever your chosen agent CLI costs you: it runs on your existing subscription or API credits. Normal distillation estimates the invocation count up front; strict retry lists the selected operations and local repairs. `--dry-run` prints the plan without model calls or writes. Checkpoints let an interrupted run reuse completed work. Bounded validation retries and windowed grouping may add calls, so an operation count is not an exact provider-request count. Sessions too large for the input budget (default 400k chars, `--input-budget`) are **refused before anything is spent**. Re-run with `--truncate=extreme` to cut them (recorded in provenance) or narrow the scope. Digest and author calls run 3 at a time by default (`--concurrency`; `1` = sequential). **Subscription or API?** human-hindsight shells out to `claude -p`, `codex exec`, `kiro-cli chat`, or `opencode run`; however your chosen CLI is authenticated is how calls are billed. `--model` passes through without pinning a model version. **Why is a session missing from my exports?** Sessions with zero human messages are skipped naturally, `--min-messages` filters thin ones, and fork/resume copies are deduped into their original session. Note that dedupe is global across all projects: with `--project`, a message duplicated by fork/resume is attributed to its earliest session even when that session is outside the filter. Run `export --verbose` to see every dropped piece with a reason. If genuine human input was dropped, that's a bug: file an extraction-fidelity report. **Can I regenerate everything from scratch?** `human-hindsight distill --fresh` clears the checkpoints (after confirming) and re-runs. Old library entries from previous generations are flagged as orphans in `status`. ## Roadmap - Claude Code **plugin packaging** for existing marketplaces (for distribution, without standing up a separate marketplace) - An in-session **skill variant** ("distill this session as we go") - **Agent SDK** orchestration exploration - **parentUuid-aware anaphora** (branch-correct antecedents on forked conversations) - **`--redact` patterns** for exports - An opt-in **community oneshot showcase** ## Development ```bash npm install npm test # vitest: fixtures only, never reads your agent stores npm run lint # biome npm run typecheck # tsc --noEmit npm run build # tsdown → dist/ ``` See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), especially the guide to adding a fixture when you hit an unhandled transcript shape. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) ## Author Built by [Aditya Singhal](https://adityasinghal.com). If human-hindsight surfaces a pattern you didn't know you had, [I'd love to hear about it](https://github.com/adityaarunsinghal/human-hindsight/issues).
